The typical energy requirements for ethane liquefaction facilities, generally combined with a natural 61 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. gas liquid fractionation plant, vary between 0.3 and 0.5 kWh/kg of LE (Sabbagh, Fanaei, and Arjomand 2020) depending on the process design, type of refrigerant used, and plant capacity. 4.1.6 General Liquefied Ethane Delivery Methods LE delivery technology combines advanced cryogenic engineering and special distribution infrastructure for the safe and efficient transport of ethane from production sources to end users. Commonly, ethane is separated from natural gas in processing plants and is liquefied by cooling down to around −90°C (183 K) for bulk transport and storage. This drastically reduces its volume, thus making it suitable for delivery across dedicated pipelines and transport by ship or rail when there are no feasible pipeline connections. Figure 41. Natural gas liquid pipeline network in the United States. Source: Nichols (2019) The United States has dedicated ethane delivery pipelines, primarily serving the major petrochemical and energy production regions, shown in Figure 41. This sophisticated network connects ethane production areas, primarily from natural gas processing plants in major shale regions, to chemical plants, fractionation facilities, storage terminals, and export docks. The use of ethane pipelines enables efficient, high-volume transport at relatively low cost and environmental impact compared to alternatives like trucking or rail, which are used where pipeline connections are not feasible. These pipelines handle large volumes of purified ethane, transporting it from processing and fractionation plants to chemical plants, storage facilities, or export terminals for shipment abroad. Modern ultra-large ethane carriers that are cargo ships with specialized gas vessels represent the most efficient and technologically sophisticated way of moving such cargo. The design includes several layers of insulation and a stainless steel primary barrier that prevents leakage with very minimal heat ingress from the surrounding environment. By minimizing the amount of external heat into the cargo tanks, these systems significantly reduce the generation of boil-off gas. Because ethane has a higher boiling point than methane, ultra-large ethane carriers do not require as much insulation thickness as LNG carriers. This allows the use of lighter and more space- efficient cargo tanks, increasing storage capacity without sacrificing safety or thermal efficiency. The consequences are lower overall transportation costs and better energy utilization throughout the shipping cycle. The ultra-large ethane carriers have a sophisticated boil-off gas management 62 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. system, including subcoolers, high-pressure pumps, and vaporizers, which keeps the ethane in a fully liquefied state throughout the voyage. All vaporized ethane from the cargo tanks is collected, reliquefied, and returned into storage to avoid cargo loss.
